chapters.body:
The handle itself is a small disclosure. @aleabitoreddit — a Latinate rendering of "Reddit player" — announces a provenance that the account simultaneously claims and chafes against. The bio reads: "That famous @Reddit WSB Trader now on X. AI/Semi Supply Chain Analyst ex. RISC-V FDN, AI research scientist; now trading unknown bottlenecks." No verified surname appears anywhere in the public record. The display name is Serenity.

The account's first posts, in July 2025, did not suggest what was coming. One early thread mapped a Naruto storyline onto an Upwork (UPWK) price chart and concluded, drily, that the bull pattern was visible to "anyone with a PHD such as myself." The ironic register was a deliberate riff on the WallStreetBets aesthetic of mock-academic retail trading. By September 2025 the tone had shifted: Serenity was posting 195 tweets a month on *indium phosphide* wafer supply, *co-packaged optics* (the integration of optical transceivers directly onto a compute chip's package), and the capital-expenditure guidance of Korean memory manufacturers. By March 2026 the monthly count had reached 994.

The WallStreetBets provenance is unverifiable in its specifics. No public Reddit archive or media report documents a notable WSB figure matching Serenity's described background. What the account has said is that it was banned from r/WallStreetBets after AXT (AXTI) rose from $12 to over $80 "because Mods got mad it kept going up and played out correctly." The username implies prior activity on the platform; the ban story implies a traceable record. Neither constitutes independent confirmation of celebrity status within that community.

## A technical background that partly checks out

The biography's claim of "ex. RISC-V FDN, AI research scientist" is more specific than most X biographies and more checkable — and it partly holds up. In a March 2026 thread, Serenity described their trajectory in semiconductor circles:

> My first job was $INTC but I quit after a really short time. Spend a year or two working on RISC-V related stuff like RocketChip, secure enclaves etc. at UC Berkeley. Was a researcher at…

The tweet was truncated in capture. But *RocketChip* is a real artifact: the Berkeley RISC-V processor generator developed in the ASPIRE Lab under Krste Asanović, the open-source implementation that underpins much of the RISC-V ecosystem and eventually anchored SiFive. Involvement at Berkeley in that period is a specific, checkable claim rather than vague credential-dropping. A later post was more emphatic: "I literally pioneered RISC-V architecture implementations back when I was at Berkeley and still hold active patents. Frontier labs and $NVDA tried recruiting me to lead some AI teams. Yet the only mention of my background is 'WSB meme…'"

RISC-V International does not publish historical working-group or staff rosters, so the "ex. RISC-V FDN" designation cannot be confirmed against a public membership list. The broader academic trail has some independent corroboration: @SingularityRes, a separate account in the wider photonics cluster, noted in April 2026 that "Serenity has a paper in Nature," a claim Serenity acknowledged in kind ("I went to UC Berkeley and I have nature publications as well"). The account also describes holding patents in semiconductors and cryptography, and lists its current occupation as running a fintech company whose name does not appear in any public corporate filing.

The technical background is self-reported at several links in the chain. It is nonetheless more substantive than the WSB-influencer framing that critical press coverage has reflexively reached for.

## The analytical method

The conceptual frame is simple enough to state in a sentence: find the *functional monopoly* — a small supplier whose process IP, geography or capacity reservation makes it impossible to substitute on any commercially relevant timeframe — before institutions do. The logic is that a bottleneck at a sub-$2bn supplier is more dangerous to a hyperscaler's product roadmap than any GPU substitution risk, and therefore eventually commands a price that reflects the ransom value, not a standard earnings multiple. Serenity is explicit that conventional valuation metrics misread this dynamic:

> Stop trying to model bottlenecks with traditional metrics like P/S or P/E… For $AXTI: it's like you found a restroom after eating 20 Tacos with Pinto Beans from Taco Bell. You're out of the toilet paper… but it's urgent.

The irreverence is calibrated. Posts mix supply-chain topology maps, translated Japanese regulatory filings, and meme-adjacent language in proportions that appear designed to maximise engagement without surrendering analytical substance. The February and March 2026 posting surge — 692 and 994 tweets respectively — coincided with NVIDIA's (NVDA) GTC event and the first broad market recognition of co-packaged optics as a commercial reality.

## Reception and scepticism

The account's growth from effectively zero to roughly 230,000 followers in under ten months generated its own secondary literature. @SingularityRes captured the dynamic in April 2026: "every retail optics investor is a @aleabitoreddit wrapper." @Ren_aramb, whose own account grew in the same period, called Serenity "the godfather of FinX" and "my main source of alpha." @ParadisLabs, a regular interlocutor on thesis posts, described Serenity as having covered certain names better than it probably could itself.

Scepticism exists, too. @MoodyWriter13, who describes a claimed offline acquaintance — an "actor colleague from that short film" — and who Serenity has since blocked, raised a pointed structural challenge: if Sivers Semiconductors (SIVE.ST) is as critical to the CPO laser supply chain as presented, why have strategic buyers not taken equity stakes? The question remains open. MoodyWriter13 also disputed Serenity's characterisation of Riber (ALRIB.PA), arguing that utilisation was running at 50–60% and meaningful demand ramp was years away.

Serenity's self-reported performance figures vary depending on which post you read: 630% YTD in early 2026, then 1,337% and 1,525% as additional names paid off. An independent reconstruction of publicly-timestamped calls, applied on an equal-weight basis to 160 trades across 200 unique tickers, reaches approximately 570% over a 213-day window — consistent with the thesis having worked, while leaving total returns a function of position sizing that cannot be reconstructed from public posts alone.

chapters.title: The ‘functional monopolies’ worldview
chapters.lede: The organising principle behind Serenity’s portfolio is not a bet on AI growth but on supply chain geography: the conviction that the compute buildout concentrates economic value at obscure, hard-to-replicate chokepoints that institutional analysts have not yet mapped. The term ‘functional monopolies’ crystallises that conviction into an investable frame. What the frame means, which companies it covers, and where it bends under pressure reveals as much about Serenity’s method as about any individual stock.
chapters.body:
## The anatomy of a chokepoint

Serenity’s self-described investment edge is simple enough to fit in a sentence. “It’s just investing in supply chains and finding chokepoints in them that markets might not realize yet.” What that sentence papers over is a taxonomy and a selection discipline that determine whether any given chokepoint is worth owning — and for how long.

The shorthand that has come to define the portfolio is “functional monopolies,” a term Serenity first applied to TOWA Corporation (6315.T) and MSSCorp (6830.T) before consolidating the concept into a canonical list on April 29th, 2026:

> I’m personally a fan of the functional monopolies. Here’s 6 of them that I own. 1. $TOWA (6315) — HBM4 Compression 2. MSSCorp (6830) — CPO Inspection 3. $LPK — Glass Core Substrates 4. $SOI — Silicon Photonics Substrates 5. $AXTI — End-to-End (mineral, refinery, production) InP

The post, truncated at Twitter’s character limit, nominates six positions but reveals only five. Context across the feed — repeated descriptions of Sivers Semiconductors (SIVE.ST) as “the next chokepoint” in continuous-wave DFB lasers for co-packaged optics — suggests SIVE was the intended sixth.

The word “functional” is doing meaningful work in the phrase. None of these companies holds a legal monopoly. The claim is instead about practical market control at a single indispensable process layer: whether the sole qualified supplier at that layer could be substituted within any commercially relevant timeframe. The geopolitical frame is explicit: “The World is fighting over oil, rare earths, and semiconductors. Every supply chain is being weaponised right now. And it so happens, US biggest geopolitical enemies own most of the chokepoints.”

## Five layers and a taxonomy

The five disclosed positions span distinct stages of the AI hardware value chain. Serenity draws a further distinction — between a *bottleneck* and a *chokepoint* — that determines holding period. “These are chokepoints over multiple year supercycles not bottlenecks,” Serenity wrote in April. “Stuff like glass core or dfb lasers should scale past 2028 and this is the beginning of the next volume ramp from architectural shifts in photonics.”

A bottleneck, in this taxonomy, is a near-term supply squeeze solvable with capital and time. AXT Inc (AXTI), which supplies *indium phosphide* (InP) substrates — the crystalline base material required for high-speed optical transceivers and photonic integrated circuits — is the clearest example: genuinely scarce today, but expandable in principle. A chokepoint is structural: process IP that takes years to qualify at customer fabrication lines, regardless of competing capital expenditure. LPKF Laser & Electronics (LPK.DE), which controls *laser-induced deep etching* (LIDE) technology for drilling fine vias in glass core substrates, exemplifies the latter. Its largest known production partner is Onto Innovation (ONTO), and the technology is proprietary to a degree that makes qualification timelines — not capital — the binding constraint.

Soitec (SOI.PA) occupies a comparable position at the substrate layer of silicon photonics. Soitec’s management has stated publicly that their Photonics-SOI products are “deployed in 100% of next-generation AI data centers” — a claim Serenity cites repeatedly as straightforward validation. TOWA Corporation, at roughly $1.35 billion in market capitalisation at initiation, dominates compression moulding for HBM4 (*high-bandwidth memory*, fourth generation), with Micron (MU), SK Hynix (000660.KS), and Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) as primary customers. MSSCorp, initiated in late April 2026, targets ninety percent of the *co-packaged optics* (CPO) inspection market — a figure the company itself publicised — and prompted the clearest articulation of the functional-monopoly concept: “This appears to be a functional monopoly in CPO for inspection.”

AXT is analytically the most demanding case. Serenity argues it spans four separate chokepoints under one corporate roof: mineral feedstock procurement, pyrolytic boron nitride crucibles used in substrate growth, bulk InP substrate production, and epiwafer deposition. The analogy deployed is deliberately arresting:

> Introducing the Strait of $AXTI: 20% of the world’s total global oil supply passes through the Strait of Hormuz. It is the single most critical chokepoint in the global energy trade.

## Intellectual priors and the limits of the frame

The structural insight underlying the thesis — that AI hardware dependency is concentrated in ways not yet reflected in equity prices — overlaps with supply chain mapping published by SemiAnalysis and with Leopold Aschenbrenner’s *Situational Awareness* essay, which Serenity explicitly cites, though with disagreements on specific names. Where the approach diverges is in declining to model the concentration rigorously. “It’s impossible to model forward revenue for new bottlenecks/chokepoints like $AXTI or $SIVE,” Serenity acknowledges; the substitute is qualitative conviction about structural position, amplified by speed of discovery ahead of institutional coverage.

That argument is exposed to two failure modes Serenity has identified but not fully resolved. The first is design-out risk: Himax Technologies (HIMX) appeared to control the micro-lens array supply chain for early photonics modules, then fell 31.5%. “Chokepoints can be designed out,” was the explicit lesson drawn; so was the corollary that a chokepoint “may not be material enough to translate into revenue like $AXTI.” The second is pricing-power latency. A recurring observation in the AXT threads — part irony, part genuine analysis — is that the company’s structural position would be worth multiples more if management exercised pharmaceutical-style pricing discipline: “I would be more bullish on $AXTI if Martin Shkreli joined the board to show em how it’s done when you have a monopoly.” A functional monopoly that does not extract monopoly rents is, for the equity investor, considerably less interesting than the structural position alone implies.

The ‘functional’ qualifier distinguishes structural supply-chain positions — where no qualified substitute exists within a commercially relevant horizon — from transient pricing power or regulatory protection. The critical tests are: Can the position be designed out? Does it translate into material revenue?

In Serenity’s taxonomy, a bottleneck is a near-term supply squeeze tied to demand exceeding existing capacity — solvable with capex and time. A chokepoint is a structural process-IP position that persists across multiple technology generations, where even well-funded competition faces multi-year customer qualification cycles before becoming viable. AXT (AXTI) is classified a bottleneck; LPKF (LPK.DE) and Soitec (SOI.PA) are classified chokepoints.

An emerging chip packaging architecture in which optical transceivers and switching silicon are integrated into a single package, dramatically reducing the latency and power consumption of data-centre interconnects compared with pluggable optics. CPO is the primary demand driver Serenity cites for photonics substrates, continuous-wave lasers, and inspection equipment in the next architectural cycle.

A III-V semiconductor compound that forms the crystalline substrate for high-speed optical transceivers and photonic integrated circuits. InP substrates require specialised feedstocks (indium metal, red phosphorus), high-temperature growth crucibles, and epitaxial deposition. AXT’s vertical integration across all four sub-steps is the basis of its functional-monopoly claim.

LPKF’s proprietary laser process for drilling fine-pitch through-glass vias in glass core substrates — the advanced-packaging layer that succeeds organic ABF cores in high-density interconnect applications. The technology’s long qualification cycle and IP secrecy are the primary basis for LPKF’s chokepoint claim in the next packaging transition.

The fourth generation of high-bandwidth memory, used primarily in AI accelerators. HBM4 requires compression moulding of stacked DRAM dies into a single package — the process step TOWA Corporation dominates globally, with Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung as primary customers.

chapters.title: The photonics supercycle
chapters.lede: The AI data centre does not run on silicon alone: at terabit speeds, moving data between chips requires light, not electrons. That single physics fact has made a handful of obscure substrate and laser-supply companies — largely unknown outside specialist circles — into the most consequential chokepoints in the AI hardware stack. In 2026, Serenity's photonics cluster generated some of the largest gains on the public record; this chapter traces how the thesis mapped onto the actual supply chain, and where it held.
chapters.body:
The scale of the AI data-centre build-out has exposed a problem that electrical engineers have been quietly dreading for a decade. High-speed compute clusters — the kind that train frontier language models — are no longer constrained by processor speed. They are constrained by the bandwidth and energy cost of moving data between chips. Copper wires, however short, dissipate power as heat and distort signals at terabit rates. The solution the industry is converging on is *silicon photonics*: encoding data as pulses of light on integrated optical waveguides, moving it across a rack, a row, or a data-centre floor, and converting it back to electrons at the destination. The enabling insight is that silicon can guide light efficiently. What it cannot do is generate it.

## The substrate that makes silicon photonics possible

Every silicon photonic chip, whether fabricated by Tower Semiconductor (TSEM), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM), or GlobalFoundries, begins with the same raw material: a wafer in which a thin crystalline silicon layer — roughly 220 nanometres — sits atop an insulating buried oxide. The structure is called *silicon-on-insulator*, or SOI; the optical waveguide etched into that device layer must be uniform to within a few nanometres across a 300mm wafer, or light scatters and the transceiver fails. Only one company reliably produces photonics-grade SOI at commercial volumes: Soitec (EPA:SOI), based in Grenoble.

Soitec's competitive position rests on a process it invented in the 1990s: *Smart Cut*, in which hydrogen ions are implanted into a donor silicon wafer to cleave away a precisely controlled layer, which is then bonded by molecular adhesion onto an oxidised handle wafer. The technique transfers a layer so thin and so uniform that no alternative process — epitaxial deposition, mechanical polishing — can replicate it at the tolerances photonics demands. GlobalWafers, the Taiwanese substrate group, held a Smart Cut licence until October 2023, when it was revoked after a licensing dispute (a court-sanctioned extension runs to 2027). Shin-Etsu Handotai retains a royalty licence but does not produce meaningful photonics-grade volumes. Soitec, by elimination, holds an estimated 95%-plus share of the global photonics-SOI market.

That dominance went unnoticed by equity markets for years. The photonics segment was small — comfortably below €100 million — inside a €891 million company (FY2025) whose majority revenue came from RF-SOI wafers for 5G smartphones, a market mired in inventory correction. Soitec shares bottomed at €41.77 on March 9, 2026. Serenity entered the stock around 43 euros, framing it as a substrate-level monopoly on *co-packaged optics* (CPO — the integration of optical engines directly into the switch or GPU package, eliminating high-power electrical trace runs), trading at one times book value. By May 4 the stock printed €153.55, a 517% gain year-to-date; Bloomberg had already declared Soitec Europe's best-performing stock of 2026 by mid-April. Serenity's note on that day was characteristically terse:

> I might be pretty good at this? $SOI up enormous amounts lol.

The re-rating was not pure speculation. Soitec's Edge and Cloud AI segment, which houses Photonics-SOI, grew 27–34% organically in successive quarters even as group revenue declined. Tower Semiconductor's own filings confirm the upstream demand: its silicon photonics revenue doubled from $106 million in 2024 to $228 million in 2025, and in February 2026 Tower committed $920 million in capital expenditure to expand SiPho and SiGe capacity more than five-fold by end-2026, with over 70% of that capacity already contracted or prepaid through 2028. "The extremely high adoption rate of SiPho for 1.6T transceivers, for which Tower is the primary provider," CEO Russell Ellwanger said on the earnings call — one of the more direct competitive claims in recent semiconductor history. Tower simultaneously launched a CPO Foundry service with 300mm wafer-bonding technology, positioning itself against GlobalFoundries (which enlarged its own silicon photonics footprint in November 2025 by acquiring Singapore's Advanced Micro Foundry).

The valuation, however, has run well ahead of the revenue. At the May print, Soitec traded at roughly 394 times trailing earnings against a semiconductor sector average near 29, with revenues still declining at the group level year-on-year. Serenity offered a measured ceiling: "I don't see $SOI becoming a $40B company, maybe $8–12B in a year." At the May 4 print the market capitalisation was already €5.3 billion.

## The laser problem

Silicon photonics can guide and modulate light, but silicon cannot generate it. The physics are unaccommodating: silicon is an *indirect-bandgap* material whose electrons do not recombine radiatively. Every silicon photonic transceiver — whether pluggable or co-packaged — requires an external laser source made from *indium phosphide* (InP), a III-V compound semiconductor whose direct bandgap makes it the natural material for data-centre lasers operating in the O- and C-band.

NVIDIA (NVDA) signalled precisely where it considers the supply chain most exposed on March 2, 2026, when it announced simultaneous strategic investments of $2 billion each into Coherent Corp (NYSE:COHR) and Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE), each paired with multi-year, multi-billion-dollar purchase commitments. The two companies are respectively the largest and second-largest integrated photonics suppliers, each operating InP fabrication lines. Jensen Huang described the commitment as ensuring that "optical interconnects and advanced package integration are foundational to the next phase of AI infrastructure."

Coherent committed to doubling its six-inch InP wafer output — across fabs in Sherman, Texas and Tarfala, Sweden — one quarter ahead of schedule. Its most recent quarterly revenue reached $1.81 billion, with data-centre optical networking up 37% year-on-year. The company raised its estimate of the co-packaged optics serviceable addressable market to $15 billion at OFC 2026, where it also showcased 800G and 1.6T modulators and 400 mW continuous-wave lasers. Lumentum, for its part, posted Q3 FY2026 revenue of $808 million — up 90% year-on-year — with 200G *externally modulated laser* (EML) revenue more than doubling sequentially and laser chip shipments up sharply versus a year earlier. The company has acquired a fifth InP fab in Greensboro, North Carolina (converted from GaAs), though management does not expect material contribution until early 2028.

Serenity placed both companies firmly in the Compounders column — reliable, capital-intensive quality businesses — rather than the high-beta rockets that generated the headline returns. The assignment proved accurate: Coherent's alpha against the wider market was positive but moderate (0.31 in the dossier model), and Serenity's tier rating for the stock was explicitly Bearish relative to the smaller names, reflecting a view that the large-caps would be bid up faster than the residual upside justified.

## Upstream: substrates and epi-wafers

The InP laser supply chain has its own upstream chokepoints. Lasers begin as *epitaxial wafers*: thin stacks of precisely doped crystalline layers grown on InP substrates. Two companies sit at critical points in this chain, and both attracted early attention from Serenity's feed.

AXT Inc (NASDAQ:AXTI) is one of the few companies that refines indium and grows the bulk InP single crystals from which substrates are sliced. In Q3 2025, InP revenue grew more than 250% sequentially to a three-year high; CEO Morris Young attributed the surge to export permits finally clearing for a backlog of significant orders. By Q1 2026, InP revenue reached $13.6 million with a backlog exceeding $100 million for the first time in the company's history. AXT raised $632.5 million in equity to double substrate capacity in 2026 and again in 2027 — a commitment that implies sustained conviction about InP demand regardless of short-term permit timing. A geopolitical wrinkle complicates the picture: the majority of AXT's crystal growth is located in Beijing, and Chinese export permits have been taking roughly 60 business days to process, adding a lead-time premium to an already stretched supply chain. The dependency is not lost on US policymakers.

IQE plc (LON:IQE) takes InP substrates and grows the epitaxial device layers on them — the active semiconductor stack on which laser junctions are defined. As the world's largest independent epi-wafer foundry, IQE occupies a position analogous to Soitec's in the silicon photonics chain: it does not make lasers, but nothing inside a data-centre laser works without what IQE makes. In April 2026 the company raised £81 million in a strategic round led by MACOM Technology Solutions, which contributed £45 million in exchange for long-term supply agreements. The connection matters: MACOM supplies continuous-wave laser dies into NVIDIA's co-packaged optics programme, drawing a direct line from IQE's Cardiff fabs to NVIDIA's Spectrum-X architecture. IQE entered 2026 with a strong order book and secured multiple Tier 1 design wins for AI and hyperscale laser and detector products; shares trade at approximately 41p on the London Stock Exchange, giving the company a market capitalisation near £545 million.

## The assemblers

Applied Optoelectronics (NASDAQ:AAOI), a Texas-based transceiver maker, experienced arguably the most straightforward AI-demand story in the cluster. FY2025 revenue reached $456 million, up 83% year-on-year; management guided FY2026 above $1.1 billion and described demand as exceeding capacity through mid-2027. The company exited Q1 2026 running at 100,000 units per month of 800G and 1.6T transceivers, targeting 650,000 per month by year-end. The stock moved from a 52-week low of $12.56 to an all-time high near $192 by early May 2026.

Fabrinet (NYSE:FN), the contract manufacturer that assembles optical transceivers at its Thailand and California campuses, crossed $1 billion in quarterly revenue in Q2 fiscal 2026 — up 36% year-on-year — and is sole-source manufacturer for NVIDIA's Blackwell-generation 1.6T transceivers. Serenity accorded Fabrinet only a C-tier, reflecting the view that contract manufacturing margins, however durable, do not offer the same structural leverage as owning a functional monopoly in a substrate or material.

## Sivers and the small-cap premium

The largest single-name gain in the photonics cluster — and by portfolio metrics the best trade in Serenity's 2026 record — was Sivers Semiconductors AB (STO:SIVE). Its shares rose from roughly SEK 4 at the start of 2026 to SEK 55.95 by early May, approximately 1,247% year-to-date. Serenity first mentioned the name in March 2026 and accumulated the highest conviction score (43, S-tier) in the entire xalpha model.

Sivers designs and manufactures *distributed feedback* (DFB) laser dies — the individual light-source elements that go into data-centre transceivers and automotive LiDAR systems. Its scale is modest: FY2025 revenue was SEK 304 million (roughly $33 million at prevailing exchange rates), with an after-tax loss of SEK 186 million. The April 2026 directed share issue at SEK 14.50 — well below the market price at that point — raised SEK 125 million in necessary dilutive capital; investors appear to have forgiven the dilution given subsequent price action. Alongside a 1.6T *linear drive optical* (LRO) module collaboration with Jabil announced in April 2026 and a LiDAR ramp with up to $138 million in cumulative lifetime revenue targeted for Q4 2026, Sivers has agreements with POET Technologies (NASDAQ:POET) for InP DFB laser arrays targeting CPO modules, and a parallel arrangement with O-Net and Enablence Technologies for *external light source* (ELS) assemblies.

The POET partnership briefly became an object lesson in single-customer concentration risk. POET's largest announced customer, Marvell Technology (which had acquired Celestial AI), cancelled all outstanding purchase orders on April 23, 2026, citing a confidentiality breach. POET shares fell roughly 50% in a week. The episode mattered to the Sivers thesis — Sivers held its own POET partnership — but the practical effect on Sivers' order book was limited, and shares held their broader trajectory. POET itself was pre-revenue at commercial scale ($1.07 million in FY2025 revenue against $63 million in net losses), which made the cancellation existential in tone even as the company moved to disclose a separate $5 million production order and maintained existing partnerships. A well-regarded sceptic noted as early as mid-April that Sivers was "trading at a ~$1B market cap with just ~$30M in 2025 revenue... largely on speculation, with no formal forward guidance." That remains a fair characterisation of the residual risk even after the 2026 run.

## Adjacent plays: Credo and the copper alternative

Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) occupies a useful conceptual boundary for the cluster. Its *active electrical cables* (AECs) — copper cables with on-board retimer chips that regenerate signals at both ends — do not use photonics at all. Within the scale-up fabric connecting GPUs inside a single training cluster, distances are often under three metres — short enough that AECs outperform pluggable optics on cost, power, and latency. Credo's Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue reached $407 million, up 201% year-on-year, and the company now serves all five major domestic hyperscale customers. The counter-narrative embedded in that figure is that the transition to co-packaged optics inside the GPU cluster, though widely anticipated by the photonics community, has not yet materialised in purchasing decisions. CPO's arrival will eventually cannibalise AECs in the scale-up fabric; the uncertainty is when. Serenity assigned Credo a C-tier, reflecting limited conviction relative to the substrate and laser supply names.

## What held up

The technical record supports three of Serenity's structural claims. Soitec genuinely holds a functional monopoly on photonics-grade SOI — a fact that Tower's $920 million capex plan and TSMC's COUPE (Compact Universal Photonic Engine) co-packaged optics platform jointly confirm. InP laser supply was, as argued across repeated posts, the binding constraint that NVIDIA's $4 billion dual investment was designed to address. And Tower's silicon photonics capacity was indeed being contracted years in advance, not speculated about.

The fourth claim — that CPO adoption would pull the small-cap laser suppliers into hyperscaler supply chains at volume — is more contested. Co-packaged optics remains a 2027–2028 volume story for most of the cluster. What made the trade work in 2026 was that the market re-rated the option value of those positions months before CPO revenues materialised on schedule. Serenity's own taxonomy — rockets versus compounders — implies the cluster was never a single bet, and the portfolio record suggests the distinction was well-chosen.

> Maybe here's what I'd do personally: "High Upside Rockets": 1. $SIVE 2. MSSCorp 3. PCL 4. $AAOI Compounders: 1. Shunsin 2. Sumitomo 3. Furukawa 4. $COHR 5. $LITE

concepts.definition: A technology that uses silicon-based waveguides to guide and modulate light on a chip, enabling high-speed, low-power optical data links between processors. Because silicon is transparent to infrared light and compatible with standard semiconductor fabrication, it allows optical functions to be integrated alongside electronics on the same wafer.

A wafer structure in which a thin crystalline silicon layer (typically 220 nm for photonics) sits atop an electrically insulating buried oxide. The index contrast between the silicon device layer and the oxide below confines light within the waveguide, which is essential for low-loss optical routing on a photonic chip.

Soitec's proprietary wafer-engineering process that uses hydrogen-ion implantation to cleave a precisely controlled thin layer from a donor silicon wafer, then bonds it by molecular adhesion onto a handle wafer. It is the only technique capable of producing photonics-grade SOI with the sub-nanometre thickness uniformity required across 300mm wafers at commercial volumes.

An advanced packaging architecture that integrates optical engines — lasers, modulators, and photodetectors — directly into the same package as a switch ASIC or GPU, eliminating the long electrical traces between chip and pluggable transceiver. CPO reduces power consumption and signal latency at terabit-class bandwidth, but imposes strict requirements on laser power, packaging yield, and thermal management.

A III-V compound semiconductor with a direct bandgap, enabling efficient light emission. Because silicon cannot lase, every silicon photonic transceiver requires InP-based laser dies as external light sources. InP substrates and epitaxial wafers are produced by a small number of specialist companies, creating a structural bottleneck upstream of the transceiver supply chain.

An InP laser whose cavity includes a periodic grating that selects a single emission wavelength. DFB lasers are the dominant light source in data-centre transceivers because their narrow linewidth and stable wavelength allow dense wavelength-division multiplexing, packing multiple data channels onto a single fibre.

A copper cable with integrated retimer chips at each end that regenerate digital signals electronically, extending the useful reach of copper interconnects inside server racks. AECs compete with pluggable optical transceivers for short-reach GPU-to-GPU connections in AI training clusters, and have gained significant share because CPO is not yet available at volume.

chapters.title: HBM and advanced packaging
chapters.lede: The arithmetic of modern AI hardware is straightforward: a single GB200 GPU consumes more high-bandwidth memory bandwidth than a supercomputer from a decade ago, and assembling the package that delivers that bandwidth requires a small cast of specialist suppliers who do not yet appear in most investors' research universe. Serenity's cluster of ten names maps each step in that assembly chain, from compression molding to photonic inspection to wafer-level burn-in, and in most cases identifies the sole or dominant vendor at each step.
chapters.body:
## The stacking imperative

Every H100 and GB200 GPU ships with High Bandwidth Memory arranged as stacks on a substrate the size of a thumbnail. That substrate — Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's (TSM) *CoWoS* (*Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate*) — has become, by one credible measure, the most constrained manufacturing resource in the global semiconductor industry. Epoch AI's supply chain research found that four companies consumed roughly 90% of global CoWoS capacity and 90% of global HBM supply in 2025, while drawing on less than 12% of advanced logic die production. The constraint was not the chips themselves. It was how they were stacked and wired together.

This observation sits at the core of a cluster Serenity assembled from late 2025 through early 2026: the chokepoints worth owning were not the headline chip designers but the narrow band of suppliers without whom the package cannot be assembled. The ten names — **TOWA** (6315.T), **MSSCorp** (6830.T), Aehr Test Systems (AEHR), SanDisk (SNDK), Micron Technology (MU), KLA Corporation (KLAC), Onto Innovation (ONTO), Applied Materials (AMAT), Lam Research (LRCX) and Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) — map almost exactly onto the bill of materials for a CoWoS HBM package.

## The specification inflection

The JEDEC HBM4 standard (JESD270-4), finalized in April 2025, doubled the per-stack memory interface from 1,024 to 2,048 bits, raising peak bandwidth from approximately 1.2 terabytes per second for HBM3E to 2 terabytes per second. The standard is not backward-compatible with HBM3E controllers, meaning every AI chip designed around NVIDIA's Vera Rubin requires a new physical-layer interface, a new interposer design and new packaging equipment. The HBM market grew from $18 billion in 2024 to $35 billion in 2025 — a 94% increase — driven almost entirely by AI training.

Micron Technology (MU) entered HBM4 mass production in Q2 calendar 2026, shipping 12-Hi stacks at pin speeds above 11 gigabits per second, ahead of the JEDEC minimum. Management confirmed that the entire calendar 2026 HBM allocation was sold under binding agreements before production began, and raised fiscal-2026 capex to $20 billion. In a structurally significant move, Micron outsourced its HBM4E base logic die to TSMC's most advanced nodes — an arrangement that ties American memory production directly to CoWoS utilization rates at Taiwan Semiconductor.

## Compression molding: the monopoly nobody talks about

TOWA (6315.T), trading at roughly ¥200 billion ($1.35 billion market cap) entering 2026, occupies an unusual competitive position. After DRAM dies are assembled via thermocompression bonding, each completed stack must be over-molded in epoxy to protect wire bonds and provide structural rigidity. TOWA claims approximately 90% of the global market for *compression molding* of HBM stacks — a share its rivals have found difficult to erode because the process requires equipment and proprietary resin formulations tuned to specific die geometries.

HBM4 introduces a precise mechanical challenge: the 2,048-bit interface requires a wider, thinner stack cross-section with less vertical clearance for encapsulant to flow into during molding. TOWA's response was *Ultra narrow gap Mold Underfill* (UMF), announced in March 2025 and positioned as the production solution for HBM4 volume assembly. The company guided FY2026 revenue to ¥71 billion ($474 million at prevailing rates), a 31% increase from the prior year, on pull from SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron's concurrent HBM3E production and HBM4 qualifications.

Serenity identified TOWA through the same monopoly-screening logic applied across their broader portfolio:

> So just putting it out there: Towa (6315), at $1.35B... Is a rare, living definition of monopoly over HBM4 (compression molding). It's been kinda flat YTD, but every memory company like $MU, SK Hynix, Samsung are their customers. And each of the memory company earnings signaled [aggressive capex].

The market was slow to respond. Despite clear upward capex signals in Micron and SK Hynix earnings, TOWA had been roughly flat through early 2026. Earnings due May 11, 2026 provided the catalyst: the stock gained over 15% in a single session on May 6, recovering toward its 52-week high. Serenity's framing was characteristically blunt elsewhere: "Names like $ONTO / $CAMT go brr. Throw in $TOWA (6315), since there's indication of aggressive memory production ramp."

## CPO inspection: MSSCorp's claimed perch

MSSCorp (6830.T), around ¥200 billion in market cap, addresses a different but adjacent chokepoint: quality control for *co-packaged optics* (CPO). CPO integrates laser transceivers directly onto the same substrate as the GPU and HBM stack — eliminating the pluggable optical module, cutting latency by roughly 10x and power consumption by roughly half for the same bandwidth. Goldman Sachs projected the total optical networking market to grow from $15 billion to $154 billion, with CPO alone contributing $91 billion of that figure. TSMC's own *COUPE* (*Compact Universal Photonic Engine*) platform, targeted for volume production in 2026, brings a photonic die onto the CoWoS substrate alongside HBM and logic — and every such die will require optical inspection to assess yield.

Serenity characterized MSSCorp as a "functional monopoly in CPO for inspection" — the verification step that determines whether CPO modules meet yield thresholds before they are assembled into expensive packages. The company stated its goal as capturing 90% of the CPO inspection market. Serenity drew an explicit distinction between materials failure analysis, an oligopoly shared with MA-tek and iST, and CPO optical inspection, the claimed single-vendor position:

> I am now long MSSCorps (6830) ~$1.4B MC. This appears to be a functional monopoly in CPO for inspection. But markets might have conflated that with Material/Failure Analysis with MA-tek and iST (oligopoly). For customers from mapping: 1. TSM 2. NVDA 3. AAPL 4. AMAT...

The research caveat is genuine. MSSCorp's primary public identity is as a materials analysis and failure analysis service provider — a close but not identical description to CPO optical inspection. If Serenity's customer-mapping exercise is correct, placing TSMC, NVIDIA and Apple as CPO inspection clients, the addressable market is substantially larger. If the distinction collapses in practice, the competitive moat is narrower than claimed.

## Aehr: testing before the expensive mistake

Aehr Test Systems (AEHR) addresses a problem that compounds with every CoWoS generation: a latent defect in a $30 silicon photonics die assembled into a $3,000 CoWoS package is a catastrophic yield event. AEHR's *FOX-XP* system performs *wafer-level burn-in* — subjecting chips to elevated voltage and temperature while still on the wafer, before dicing and packaging, precipitating early-life failures at the cheapest possible point in the manufacturing flow.

In November 2025 Aehr partnered with ISE Labs (an ASE Group subsidiary) specifically to provide *known-good-die* (KGD) screening for silicon photonics dies destined for CoWoS integration, naming CoWoS explicitly as the target package. In March 2026 a major global networking supplier ordered high-power FOX-XP systems rated at 3,500 watts per wafer for silicon photonics transceiver burn-in at hyperscale data centres.

Serenity's initial framing was deliberately speculative:

> I'm actually long $AEHR right now in the event any of the big three memory companies use them for HBM DRAM die burn in or hyperscalers expand Sonoma usage. Then there's silicon photonics, which is another area of interest. So it's more of a speculative moonshot pick to see if [they win the silicon photonics business].

The silicon photonics leg moved faster than the HBM memory leg. Quarterly bookings reached $37.2 million in Q3 FY2026, a book-to-bill above 3.5x. Serenity later described AEHR as "one of my favorite longs" with an expected inflection comparable to what they had seen in optical transceiver names. The dossier records 80% alpha above the market during the holding window — a tier-A signal in the broader reconstruction.

## SanDisk: the inference detour

SanDisk (SNDK), spun off from Western Digital in February 2025 as a pure-play NAND vehicle, is the cluster's most anomalous name. It is not an HBM company. Its stacked NAND architecture — built on BiCS *Complementary Bit-Cost Scalable* (CBA) wafer bonding — targets inference workloads where capacity (up to 512 gigabytes per stack under the proposed High Bandwidth Flash standard) matters more than the sub-nanosecond latency that HBM provides. In August 2025 SanDisk and SK Hynix signed a memorandum to jointly define the HBF specification, with first samples expected in H2 2026.

The thesis Serenity applied was more direct: SNDK was a NAND supercycle position, re-rated to semiconductor multiples following the spinoff from a hardware-manufacturer parent. They reported feeling FOMO watching the chart daily, eventually averaging into the position at around \$540 after a 7% pullback, describing it as "a possible $NVDA for me at $79B — fundamentals matter more to me than short term supply events." Gross margins expanded from the low 20s to approximately 78% in Q3 fiscal 2026 as the product mix shifted toward high-margin QLC NAND. The stock exceeded 2,400% from spinoff through spring 2026.

## The equipment layer

KLA Corporation (KLAC), Onto Innovation (ONTO), Applied Materials (AMAT) and Lam Research (LRCX) are not chokepoints in the same narrow sense as TOWA. They are the machinery that builds the chokepoints. Their revenue scales directly with the pace of CoWoS and HBM capacity expansion.

KLA reported approximately $950 million in advanced packaging revenue in calendar 2025, roughly 80% above 2024, and has guided the segment to continued elevated growth. Its process control tools — covering *through-silicon via* (TSV) quality, bump coplanarity before bonding and overlay registration in CoWoS interposers — are more heavily consumed per wafer as HBM die count and package complexity increase. Management noted that HBM devices create "higher process control opportunities" because the reliability specification, not merely the yield target, demands tighter defect budgets at each stacking step.

Onto Innovation (ONTO) signed a volume purchase agreement exceeding $240 million with a leading HBM manufacturer for Dragonfly 2D inspection and 3D bump metrology systems through 2027 — the largest single packaging-specific tool contract publicly disclosed in the industry. Its Dragonfly 3Di sub-surface inspection system, capable of detecting micro-cracks from thinning and bonding at production throughput, was qualified at two major HBM customers during the period. The company guided advanced packaging revenue growth of over 30% for 2026.

Applied Materials (AMAT) occupies the broadest position in the cluster. Its Kinex *hybrid bonding* system, co-developed with Besi and launched in October 2025, is the first fully integrated die-to-wafer hybrid bonder in commercial production, placing 1,600 dies per hour with on-board metrology at bump pitches below 4 microns. Hybrid bonding replaces solder bumps with direct copper-to-copper interconnects and is the intended production technology for HBM4E. In May 2026 AMAT acquired NEXX from ASMPT for $120 million to add panel-level electrochemical deposition capability, anticipating the transition from CoWoS wafer format to 510×515mm panel format (TSMC's *CoPoS* platform) targeted for mass production around 2028.

Lam Research (LRCX) anchors the deposition side. Its SABRE 3D copper plating system revenues more than doubled in calendar 2024 on CoWoS *redistribution layer* (RDL) copper plating demand; its Aether dry photoresist was selected as production tool-of-record at a leading HBM manufacturer in January 2025, meaning each successive DRAM node refresh carries increasing Lam content per wafer. Management guided "well over $3 billion" in combined GAA-plus-advanced-packaging shipments for 2025.

Serenity identified the equipment group as downstream beneficiaries rather than lead convictions, noting: "I feel like $TSM and OSAT/advanced packaging partners are the main beneficiaries... maybe like $AMAT, $LRCX, $KLAC, $ASML and others too."

## Tower Semiconductor and the photonic layer

Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) connects the HBM cluster to the photonics architecture covered separately in this report: as the leading independent foundry for silicon photonics dies, it makes the optical engines that TSMC's COUPE platform will integrate onto CoWoS substrates alongside HBM stacks and GPU logic. Serenity's framing was succinct — "I'm long $TSEM, the $TSM of photonics" — and they took an initial position after a 21% decline in March 2026; the stock doubled in a month.

The structural logic underlying the cluster runs in a single direction: TOWA molds the HBM stack, MSSCorp inspects the photonic module, AEHR burns in the photonic dies before assembly, and Tower makes the dies that AEHR tests. Capacity constraints anywhere in that chain become yield constraints everywhere. That is, stripped of its WSB cadence, the observation Serenity has been making since late 2025 — and the reason the cluster, taken together, carries the kind of specificity that distinguishes a supply-chain thesis from a generalized bet on AI hardware spend.

concepts.definition: TSMC's advanced 2.5D packaging platform that places multiple chiplets — GPU logic, HBM memory stacks, and increasingly photonic dies — side by side on a shared silicon interposer, which is then mounted on a conventional organic substrate. CoWoS allows far shorter electrical distances between chips than a standard PCB, enabling the high bandwidth required by modern AI accelerators.

DRAM in which multiple dies are stacked vertically using through-silicon vias, then placed directly adjacent to the processor on a shared interposer. The wide parallel interface (1,024 bits per stack for HBM3E, 2,048 bits for HBM4) delivers bandwidth that far exceeds conventional DDR5, at the cost of a more complex and expensive packaging process.

An architecture that integrates optical transceivers — the devices that convert electrical signals to photons for transmission over fibre — directly onto the same package substrate as the processor, rather than in a separate pluggable module. CPO reduces latency by roughly 10x and power consumption by roughly half at equivalent bandwidth, and is considered the likely successor to pluggable optics in hyperscale AI data centres from 2026 onwards.

The manufacturing step in which a completed HBM die stack is sealed inside an epoxy compound using a press that applies the resin from above under controlled pressure and temperature, rather than injecting it from the side as in transfer molding. Compression molding is preferred for HBM because it applies lower mechanical stress to the thin stacked dies and achieves better surface flatness, which is critical for subsequent bonding to the GPU interposer.

A die that has been tested and burned-in at the wafer level before being diced and assembled into a multi-chip package. KGD screening is increasingly important as CoWoS packages become more expensive: assembling a defective die into a package worth hundreds or thousands of dollars destroys the value of all the other known-good components in that package.

A die-stacking technique that forms direct copper-to-copper electrical connections between dies without solder bumps, enabling interconnect pitches below 4 microns — roughly 10x finer than current micro-bump technology. Hybrid bonding is the roadmap path for HBM4E and beyond, promising higher bandwidth density and lower power consumption per bit transferred between the memory and logic dies.

Thin copper wiring layers deposited on an interposer or reconstituted wafer that route electrical signals between the fine-pitch bumps of a chiplet and the coarser-pitch bumps that connect to the organic substrate. In CoWoS interposers, multiple RDL layers carry high-density signal routing between GPU logic and HBM stacks; their fabrication requires precise copper plating and etch steps.

A vertical electrical connection drilled through a silicon die and filled with copper, allowing signals and power to pass between stacked dies without routing around the chip edge. TSVs are the enabling technology for HBM stacking: each DRAM die in a stack has thousands of TSVs that must be formed, inspected and precisely aligned before bonding.

chapters.title: AI infrastructure and the neoclouds
chapters.lede: In the autumn of 2025, as combined hyperscaler capital-expenditure pledges for the year crested a quarter of a trillion dollars, a new investable category was crystallising around the AI buildout: the neocloud. Serenity committed more than $1.5 million to a ranked basket of GPU-rental platforms and miner-to-HPC pivots, framing the trade as a direct downstream play on hyperscaler overflow demand. By spring 2026 the cluster had gone quiet — not because the thesis was wrong, but because the discrimination within it had already been made.
chapters.body:
## The neocloud hypothesis

In late September 2025, Serenity posted what would become the cluster's founding document:

> The NeoCloud Thesis: Hyperscaler Capex Funnel. Why I'm putting $1.5M+ into Neoclouds, and why this might be a 200–300%+ return.

The bucket structure was revealing: “Mag7 contracts” covered CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius Group (NBIS), and Cipher Digital (CIFR); “with compute” captured IREN Limited (IREN) and bitcoin miners including Bitfarms; a third tier was labelled “speculative.” The thesis rested on a single mechanic — hundreds of billions in hyperscaler capital expenditure had to flow somewhere, and the *neoclouds* (GPU-specialist infrastructure providers that rent accelerator capacity rather than offering the broad service catalogues of Amazon, Microsoft (MSFT), or Google) sat closest to the tap.

## Margins over megawatts

Within five weeks the basket had been sorted. By end of October 2025 Serenity had begun separating the category into qualitatively different species:

> Markets are starting to price in a divergence between AWS-style full-stack Neoclouds like $NBIS and miners such as $CIFR, $BITF, $CLSK, and others. This is the reason I sold off $IREN $WULF and others, and consolidated into Nebius. Why? Margins > Capacity.

The distinction was between *full-stack* providers — combining GPU hardware with software orchestration, storage, and managed inference — and *capacity* plays: power-dense facilities with repurposed mining rigs or bare GPU racks. Nebius Group stood as the archetype of the former. The Amsterdam-headquartered successor to Yandex’s international operations, rebuilt after a $5.4 billion divestiture of Russian domestic assets in July 2024, had been reconstituted under co-founder Arkady Volozh with deep distributed-systems engineering and a full managed-inference stack. Serenity’s twelve-month price target of $400 rested on explicit margin arithmetic:

> $NBIS is the next Microsoft in the making. Scaling from $100M quarterly revenue to $2B–3B+ in 1–2 years off 55–75% gross margin. Large ownership of next-generational companies like ClickHouse. Infrastructure of Mag7 AI Compute. Completely undervalued.

**Nebius’s** subsequently reported results offered partial corroboration: full-year 2025 revenue of $529.8 million, up 479% year-on-year, with 2026 guidance of $3.0–3.4 billion. A reported $2.7 billion infrastructure agreement with Meta, if finalised, would represent a step-function expansion beyond its existing hyperscaler base.

## The CoreWeave sceptic

CoreWeave occupied an ambiguous position from the outset — listed in the “Mag7 contracts” bucket but attracting growing scepticism as the thesis matured. The company had gone public on NASDAQ on 28 March 2025 at $40 per share, and its commercial model — long-term, debt-financed GPU-capacity contracts, often three to seven years in duration, collateralised against the GPU hardware itself — drew an analogy from Serenity that became the cluster’s most-quoted formulation. When NVIDIA (NVDA) invested $2 billion in CoreWeave at $87.20 per share in January 2026, Serenity read the move sceptically:

> A casino gives you more money, so you could take on more debt with collateral to gamble. Then all the extra money goes back to the Casino (aka. $NVDA). That doesn’t make Coreweave a good long.

By the same week, the position had turned formally short:

> $CRWV is probably the only $50B+ company I can think of that is likely going to go bankrupt. At least $ORCL has a profitable core business and owns tons of assets. Coreweave is a clear short to me purely because a large part of their revenue will be used to…

The critique was structural rather than cyclical. CoreWeave’s model requires perpetual debt refinancing to fund hardware whose replacement cycle is measured in months; Microsoft accounted for approximately 67% of FY2025 revenue of $5.1 billion, leaving the business acutely exposed to a single customer that could in principle build its own capacity. **The bear thesis has yet to resolve.** CoreWeave priced a $3.5 billion convertible notes offering in April 2026, signed a multi-year capacity deal with Anthropic, and reported total remaining performance obligations implying roughly thirteen years of revenue at current run rates — each step deepening the symbiosis with NVIDIA that Serenity had identified as the structural trap.

## The IREN about-turn

IREN Limited, rebranded from Iris Energy in November 2024, was initially held as a “compute” neocloud on the thesis that a hyperscaler contract would follow its power infrastructure. One did: a $9.7 billion, five-year GPU hosting agreement with Microsoft for 76,000 NVIDIA GB300 processors at its Childress, Texas campus. But the terms of financing the pivot mattered more than the headline. When IREN launched a $6 billion *at-the-money* equity offering in March 2026 — nearly half its then-market capitalisation — the position was closed:

> I see zero compelling case to hold $IREN. Especially given the new $6B share dilution at a $12.8B marketcap. People will likely see that marketcap inflate to $20–25B. But the value of their shares decrease over time.

The episode crystallised a principle running through the entire cluster: capacity expansion funded by equity dilution transfers value from existing shareholders to the infrastructure buildout itself. Only operators with sufficient software margin — and thus access to non-dilutive convertible financing — can compound shareholder value through the cycle. IREN’s dossier reads “BEAR” in the xalpha data despite carrying 0.76 annualised alpha — a reminder that price appreciation and thesis conviction are separable.

## Power as the hidden bottleneck

The cluster’s energy and infrastructure names — Vistra (VST), Constellation Energy (CEG), Talen Energy (TLN), Vertiv (VRT), Digital Realty (DLR), and Equinix (EQIX) — received notably lighter treatment. Serenity was candid about the coverage gap:

> I’ve heard of $NEE and $CEG but I don’t know enough about energy. So I’m just half-blindly buying the sector from other DD I’ve seen.

The logic was nonetheless coherent. Nuclear generation — the only source that simultaneously satisfies AI *baseload* requirements and corporate carbon mandates — was accumulating long-dated *power-purchase agreements* (PPAs) at rates that made each incremental contract highly accretive to earnings. **Constellation Energy** (CEG), the largest US nuclear operator with 21,000 megawatts across 21 reactors, has signed 20-year PPAs with both Microsoft and Meta that lock in revenue through the 2050s. Vistra (VST) guided 2026 adjusted EBITDA to $6.8–7.6 billion — roughly $1 billion above its 2025 range — anchored by 2.6 gigawatts of nuclear output contracted to Meta for two decades. Vertiv, which supplies power conversion and thermal management equipment for hyperscale data centres, rounds out the energy-adjacent layer as a direct beneficiary of the load growth driving those PPAs without requiring a nuclear licence.

## Silence as signal

The cluster’s zero-call stretch in the four weeks to 8 May 2026, while Serenity’s photonics and advanced-packaging coverage remained active, most likely reflects portfolio consolidation rather than thesis abandonment. The original basket — 79 calls peaking at 55 between September and October 2025 — has been thinned through deliberate attrition: IREN exited in late October and actively shorted by implication in March; CoreWeave turned short in January; energy names were always sector exposures rather than high-conviction single-stock picks; and the *colocation* tier — Cipher Digital (CIFR), Core Scientific (CORZ), and Applied Digital (APLD), hyperscaler-leased facilities that do not own the GPUs they host — attracted measured rather than concentrated conviction. What remains implicit is a position in Nebius as the canonical full-stack neocloud: a wager that the engineering depth inherited from Yandex, combined with software-defined margins the pure capacity providers cannot replicate, will produce a materially different earnings trajectory as the buildout matures.

Whether that holds depends on whether hyperscaler demand remains structurally sticky — a question Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, framed with unusual candour in early 2026, warning that the industry faced “bankruptcy risk” if revenue growth failed to keep pace with capital expenditure. **The capex funnel Serenity identified in September 2025 is still flowing.** The question is whether the pipes at the downstream end are built to last.

concepts.definition: A GPU-specialist cloud provider that rents NVIDIA accelerator capacity to AI developers and research labs, sitting between the chip manufacturers and the frontier labs. Unlike the major hyperscalers, neoclouds do not offer a broad service catalogue; their value proposition is fast access to large volumes of GPU compute, often under long-term contracts.

A neocloud that goes beyond bare GPU rental to provide software orchestration, managed storage, inference endpoints, and developer tooling. The full-stack model generates higher gross margins than raw capacity provision because customers pay for software value on top of hardware, creating switching costs that pure capacity providers lack.

An infrastructure operator that provides raw compute or power-dense colocation facilities without a proprietary software layer, often a repurposed bitcoin miner. Capacity plays rely on hyperscaler lease agreements for revenue and are subject to dilutive equity offerings to fund capital expenditure, limiting compounding for existing shareholders.

The strategic reorientation of a cryptocurrency mining company toward high-performance computing and AI workloads. Miners have power infrastructure and data-centre facilities that can be redeployed to host AI GPUs; the pivot requires either purchasing GPUs directly or signing colocation agreements with hyperscalers who supply the hardware.

A long-term contract between a power generator and a buyer — typically a hyperscaler or data-centre operator — fixing the price and volume of electricity delivery over periods of 10–20 years. Nuclear PPAs are particularly sought after because they guarantee baseload, carbon-free power at predictable cost, satisfying both reliability and sustainability requirements for AI data centres.

A data-centre hosting model in which the facility operator provides power, space, and physical infrastructure while the customer — typically a hyperscaler — installs and owns the servers and networking equipment. Colocation operators earn lease income without bearing GPU ownership or replacement risk.

chapters.title: Hyperscalers and sovereign AI
chapters.lede: When the four largest American hyperscalers collectively pledged roughly $690 billion in capital expenditure for 2026, the conventional read was euphoria for AI chipmakers. Serenity's read was more specific: the headline numbers were a demand signal for the upstream supply chains she had quietly been accumulating since mid-2025, not a reason to buy the hyperscalers themselves.
chapters.body:
When Alphabet (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), Meta Platforms (META), and Amazon.com (AMZN) reported their spring 2026 earnings, the capital-expenditure figures were extraordinary even by the standards of the AI buildout. Meta's full-year 2025 capex reached $72 billion; the company then raised its 2026 guidance to $125–145 billion. Microsoft guided for quarterly capex above $40 billion in the June quarter, implying a calendar-year run-rate near $190 billion. Alphabet logged $91 billion for 2025 and guided to roughly $175 billion for 2026. Amazon's 2025 capital spending topped $128 billion, with 2026 commitments exceeding $200 billion. Combined, the four companies had pledged around $690 billion in a single calendar year to building the infrastructure of artificial intelligence.

Serenity watched those earnings calls closely—and drew a different conclusion from them than most observers.

> I've monitored the situation for you. TLDR on hyperscaler capex spend (signal aside from $TSM). From $MSFT, $AMZN, $META earnings: Upstream semi supply chains go brrr. $META: 2026 FY capex $115–$135B, Revised Q1 ER: $125B–$145B capex raised. -> Higher component prices

The key phrase is “signal aside from $TSM.” For Serenity, hyperscaler earnings calls are not investment theses in themselves but primary data releases confirming demand for the upstream supply chains they actually own. The hyperscalers are the demand signal; the trade is in the components.

## NVIDIA and the custom-silicon challenge

This framing explains a paradox in Serenity’s public record. Nvidia (NVDA) dominates the AI accelerator market—its Blackwell GPU families are the *de facto* standard for AI training at every major hyperscaler, and its *CUDA* software ecosystem creates switching costs that competing hardware has struggled to overcome. Nvidia logged $186 billion in data-centre revenue for its fiscal year ending January 2026, up 65% year-on-year, on a forward P/E of roughly 17.5 times. Yet Serenity’s measured alpha on NVDA is a modest 0.12, well below their signal on Marvell Technology (MRVL) at 1.07.

The explanation is partly valuation—much of the obvious good news already priced in—and partly their reading of the custom-silicon shift. They named the tension explicitly in late 2025: “I can argue the bear case for $NVDA too, that hyperscalers are building their own ASICs. But in cases like these, you look at numbers rather than narrative—the backlog for Nvidia is wild.” Their resolution was to hold both: Nvidia for its installed base and CUDA lock-in, while accumulating separately the companies building the alternative trajectory.

By 2026 that alternative was fully operational. Broadcom (AVGO) was building *tensor processing units* (TPUs) for Alphabet (GOOGL) under a supply agreement extending to 2031, while simultaneously developing Meta Platforms’ (META) proprietary training chips; its first-quarter AI revenue hit $8.4 billion, up 106% year-on-year. Marvell was developing *XPUs*—custom AI accelerators—for at least three major hyperscaler customers, with a $75 billion lifetime-revenue pipeline disclosed at its 2025 investor event. Broadcom’s CEO Hock Tan has guided to $60–90 billion in AI chip revenue by 2027 from three hyperscaler customers alone. Serenity’s summary of Broadcom’s role required just four words: “Long hyperscaler ASIC.”

## Marvell: the hidden hyperscaler play

Of the two custom-silicon names, Marvell Technology (MRVL) has been Serenity’s highest-conviction call in this cluster. Their entry came in early September 2025, when the stock fell 18% following an earnings miss the market briefly treated as fundamental deterioration.

> $MRVL 18% drop after earnings was a complete overreaction. Perfect time to DCA into Marvell positions over the next month.

Marvell’s eventual FY2026 result—record revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42%, with data-centre sales reaching 74% of total—bore them out. The specific driver they tracked was Microsoft’s (MSFT) Maia custom AI accelerator, a chip built on Marvell silicon under a long-term programme. By April 2026 they had added a second hyperscaler to the thesis: “I liked $MRVL back at $80 and even here, mainly because of $MSFT Maia. But having $GOOGL as a likely customer for revenue visibility past 2028 helps a lot too. They’re really milking that Celestial acquisition.” Marvell’s Celestial division—acquired in 2021 for its custom silicon expertise—is the technical engine behind its hyperscaler XPU programmes.

Their characterisation of the broader opportunity captures its market-structure logic precisely:

> I feel like $COHR and $MRVL are the two “They Do Everything” longs. That nobody actually knows what they do if you ask them in public. $NVDA? GPUs. $INTC? Foundry. Marvell? No clue. Coherent? No clue. They’re the Deloitte of Semis.

Breadth of exposure, low retail awareness, institutional reluctance to underwrite complex stories before revenue appears: the information arbitrage is the alpha. Marvell spans optical DSPs for coherent networking, Ethernet *SerDes* components, enterprise storage controllers, and the XPU programmes that tie directly to two confirmed hyperscaler customers—with a third reportedly in development. Sell-side consensus had not fully modelled the Maia ramp when Serenity began building their position at $80.

## ARM and the CPU bottleneck

An original angle in Serenity’s framework concerns ARM Holdings (ARM). They took a position in late March 2026 when the company released new AI CPU roadmap news, framing ARM as a potential “NVDA for CPUs.” By late April they had a specific bottleneck thesis in view: Intel’s chief executive had disclosed that AI inference was pushing the CPU-to-GPU ratio from 1:8 toward 1:1, implying a structural step-up in CPU demand. “Bullish on $ARM, given the new bottleneck shifting back to CPUs,” they wrote. “I’m predicting parts of localised inference to be handled by CPUs more and more… as models like Gemma get lightweight in the future.”

The thesis has structural support: ARM’s Neoverse architecture already underpins the majority of hyperscaler custom CPU cores—AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt—and Arm projects that Arm-based designs could account for roughly 90% of host CPU deployments in custom AI ASIC servers by 2029, up from around 25% in 2025. At a forward P/E near 99 times, the valuation case is thin, and Serenity acknowledges it; they hold ARM as an option on an architecture cycle, not a value entry.

## Discounts and derivatives

Microsoft (MSFT) they approached as a contrarian entry. Spotting the stock near $372 in March 2026—briefly trading through its 200-week moving average for the first time in thirteen years, roughly 33% below its July 2025 all-time high—they went long, noting it looked “too discounted.” The logic was straightforward: a business generating $37 billion in annualised AI revenue with Azure growing 40% year-on-year warranted a better multiple than the market briefly assigned.

For *high-bandwidth memory* (HBM) exposure they turned to the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), buying 2028 leaps as a vehicle for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix without navigating Korean market access directly.

> I’m still personally long 2028 leaps on $EWY for memory exposure. Those are up over triple digits, since I expect Samsung/SK Hynix to be printing.

EWY recovered sharply from February 2026 lows that had prompted widespread “KOSPI crash bubble” commentary, validating a thesis that is at bottom simple: *HBM* demand cannot exist without the Korean memory duopoly. The trade also illustrates their preference for proxies—capturing a structural bottleneck through the most liquid available vehicle rather than navigating illiquid foreign-listed names directly. Korean-listed HBM suppliers became accessible to them via IBKR only in late April 2026, at which point they began researching direct positions.

On the broader sovereign AI buildout—Nvidia’s (NVDA) agreement with Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN to deploy hundreds of thousands of Blackwell GPUs, the European Investment Bank’s €70 billion technology commitment, India’s national compute initiative—Serenity has been largely silent as a theme. Oracle (ORCL), whose Stargate joint venture with OpenAI and SoftBank carries a $523 billion remaining-performance-obligation backlog, appears in their September 2025 watchlists but not as a primary thesis. Their reasoning is structural rather than geopolitical: sovereign capex ultimately flows through the same *CoWoS* advanced-packaging bottleneck at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM), the same EUV lithography machines from ASML Holding (ASML), and the same photonics and networking components they have catalogued since mid-2025. The map changes; the chokepoints do not.

concepts.definition: Compute Unified Device Architecture: Nvidia’s proprietary parallel-computing platform and programming model. Because virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, switching to non-Nvidia accelerators requires substantial engineering investment, creating deep customer lock-in.

A chip designed from scratch for a specific hyperscaler’s AI workloads, as opposed to a commodity GPU. Google’s TPU, Microsoft’s Maia, and Amazon’s Trainium are all XPUs. Marvell designs and manufactures XPUs for hyperscalers under long-term supply agreements.

TSMC’s advanced packaging technology that stacks logic chips and high-bandwidth memory onto a shared silicon interposer, enabling the dense GPU-plus-HBM configurations used in AI accelerators. Capacity is tightly constrained and allocated years in advance.

Stacked DRAM designed for extreme memory bandwidth rather than density. Nvidia’s H100 and H200 GPUs each carry up to 80–141 GB of HBM3/HBM3e, manufactured almost exclusively by SK Hynix and Samsung. HBM is a critical bottleneck in AI accelerator supply chains.

Semiconductor IP that converts parallel data streams to high-speed serial links for chip-to-chip and chip-to-optic interconnects inside data centres. Marvell is a leading supplier of high-speed SerDes for AI networking.

Chipmaking process that uses 13.5-nanometre light to print the finest circuit features on leading-edge semiconductors. ASML is the sole manufacturer of EUV machines; every advanced AI chip depends on them.

chapters.title: What hasn't worked
chapters.lede: A strategy built on identifying structural chokepoints in the AI supply chain carries within it three trades that went wrong in instructively different ways. The losses — headlined by an 84-percent wipeout in a lithium-battery meme stock — are modest in aggregate against a book of 160 trades, but their patterns reveal more than their magnitudes. They mark the outer edges of a framework: the places where Serenity stepped outside it, and what happened next.
chapters.body:
**The worst trade on the board** is Dragonfly Energy Holdings (DFLI), a Nevada-based maker of lithium-ion batteries for the RV and marine markets, entered in October 2025. It sits at the opposite end of the portfolio from everything else: no photonics, no substrate monopoly, no data-centre supply chain. The thesis was blunt:

> Saw they had military contracts, lithium battery stocks have been mooning, small 81m market cap. 28.75m raise around current prices is usually a great sign.

It was not a great sign. The $28.75 million equity raise had priced the day before at $1.25 per share — the peak of a tenfold move from summer lows. Serenity entered as the stock began its long unwinding, a descent interrupted only by a one-for-ten reverse split in December 2025. By mid-2026 the position had lost roughly 84 percent. Dragonfly's full-year 2025 results told the underlying story: revenue of $58.6 million against a net loss of $70.8 million, with *direct-to-consumer* sales falling 18 percent in the fourth quarter. No post-mortem tweet on DFLI has appeared on Serenity's feed; the silence is its own form of testimony.

The VST position — expressed not directly in Vistra Corp (VST) shares but through long-dated options on the utilities exchange-traded fund XLU — came with unusual self-awareness baked in. On entering in February 2026, they wrote:

> I'm doing DCA options because I don't know individual companies like VST well enough to pick which one is the best. But energy/utilities sector as a whole should go up as AI DCs use up a ton.

The framing was honest: buy the sector, not the stock, using XLU's unusually low *implied volatility* (roughly 14 percent) as a structural argument for cheap optionality. The thesis — that AI data-centre electricity demand represented a secular re-rating of the US utility sector — was coherent. When DeepSeek's efficient inference architecture rattled power-demand assumptions in early 2026, VST fell roughly 25 percent from its highs and the XLU options position ended underwater by roughly nine percent. The thesis may not be wrong; it may simply be early, and expensive on the way.

## The most revealing loss

Infleqtion (INFQ), a *neutral-atom* quantum-computing company that listed via a SPAC merger in February 2026, produced Serenity's most candid reckoning. They entered at $15.50 on the second day of trading, framing the stock as the first public pure-play in neutral-atom architecture — reasonably priced, they argued, against trapped-ion peers IonQ (IONQ) and Rigetti (RGTI). Within seven weeks the position was down 30 percent. On April 8th they wrote:

> my $INFQ position was down 30% or something, was a small concentration thankfully, finx influencers kept trying to convince me to go long and i gave in. should have done more dd, found much more compelling names in the sector after doing more research by myself.

The admission is striking in its precision. Serenity does not blame the market, the macro, or bad luck. They identify a process failure: social influence — the pull of their extended X network — substituted for independent analysis. The contrast with their best trades is pointed: Aehr Test Systems (AEHR), AXT (AXTI), Soitec (SOI.PA) — all were supply-chain bottleneck calls developed, as far as the record shows, ahead of crowd consensus. INFQ was the reverse: a name that arrived through the crowd.

Taken together, the three losses sketch a consistent pattern. Serenity's framework degrades predictably when they depart from it: momentum-chasing without a supply-chain anchor (DFLI), macro conviction substituting for company-level research (VST/XLU), and social consensus overriding independent work (INFQ). That they diagnose two of the three explicitly, in their own words and without much delay, suggests the lesson has landed.

concepts.definition: A qubit architecture that encodes quantum information in individual neutral atoms held in optical tweezers generated by lasers, as opposed to superconducting or trapped-ion approaches. A Special Purpose Acquisition Company is a listed blank-cheque vehicle that raises money in an IPO solely to acquire a private target. The merger with that target serves as the de facto public listing for the operating company, often at a pre-negotiated valuation and with less regulatory scrutiny than a traditional IPO.

Long-term Equity AnticiPation Securities — exchange-listed options contracts with expiration dates more than one year away. Traders use them to express directional views with defined downside risk and embedded leverage, particularly when expecting slow-moving macro trends to play out over a multi-year horizon.

The options market's forward-looking estimate of how much an asset will move, derived from current option prices rather than historical data. Low implied volatility signals that options are relatively cheap, making them attractive to buyers who anticipate an eventual large move the market has not yet priced in.

Rather than manufacturing chips, Arm charges royalties on every device that ships using an Arm-based design — from the iPhone to Android phones to embedded microcontrollers to, increasingly, cloud server chips and AI accelerators. Its v9 architecture is the basis for Apple Silicon, NVIDIA's Grace CPU, Amazon's Graviton, and the majority of mobile SoCs. Arm's business model is uniquely capital-light and royalty-compounding: as ASPs (average selling prices) of chips using Arm cores rise — driven by AI compute demand — Arm's royalty revenue grows without proportional cost increases.
module.recent: Arm trades at a forward P/E of ~98.5x on only 21.1% projected EPS growth, producing a PEG of 4.67 — the most expensive name in a table of thirty large-cap semiconductor stocks. Third-party estimates place the forward P/E even higher (90–121x as of April 2026). The premium reflects the thesis that Arm is the royalty collector of the entire AI compute era, but at a PEG of 4.67, investors are pricing in decades of compounding that has not yet materialised.
